status: drafted via multi-agent workflow, adversarially fact-checked and corrected
notes: Luke is the longest and most narratively detailed of the four Gospels, with the most extensive birth narrative of any (Zacharias, Elisabeth, Gabriel's two separate annunciations, the shepherds rather than Matthew's Magi) and a marked emphasis on the poor, women, Samaritans, and social outcasts that shapes which figures rise to full manager status here versus in Matthew. Several figures are promoted to full tiers specifically because of Luke's own unique material rather than following Matthew's precedent by default: Herod Antipas gets a full tier here (he was only a submanager under John the Baptist in Matthew) because of his expanded role across four separate scenes in this book, including the trial appearance before him found only in Luke (23:6-12); Zacchaeus, the Ten Lepers, and the raising of the Widow of Nain's son (folded into Jesus's own tier as a submanager) all reflect content unique to this Gospel. The extended scene of the sinful woman anointing Jesus's feet in the house of Simon the Pharisee (7:36-50) is likewise unique-to-Luke content; both the host and the unnamed woman are indexed as submanagers under Jesus's own tier, alongside Simon of Cyrene (23:26), who bears the cross behind Jesus toward Calvary. Three distinct women named Mary appear in this book -- the mother of Jesus, Mary Magdalene, and Mary of Bethany -- kept fully separate per the project's naming-collision rule; a fourth, Mary the mother of James, is named only at the empty tomb. At least four men named Simon appear (Peter; of Cyrene; the Pharisee; and 'called Zelotes' among the undifferentiated Other Apostles), and two men named James (the son of Zebedee, a submanager under Peter, versus the son of Alphaeus, grouped in the 'Other Apostles' collective) and two named John (the Baptist, his own full tier, versus the son of Zebedee, a submanager under Peter) are explicitly flagged apart rather than merged -- every collision case is cross-referenced via a perkNote. Anna the Prophetess is attached as a submanager under Jesus's own tier rather than Simeon's: Luke 2:25-38 depicts them as two independent witnesses in the same temple scene with no textual relationship between them, and Anna's real connection is to the infant Jesus, whom she speaks of to onlookers, not to Simeon. Because so much of Luke's most distinctive content is parables and teaching discourse rather than character-driven scenes, seven law/theme tiers carry that material (the Sermon on the Plain, the Commissioning of the Seventy, and five parable tiers -- the Good Samaritan, Parables of the Lost, Lazarus and the Rich Man, Parables of Prayer and Humility, and the Parable of the Pounds), each attributed to Jesus via deliveredBy per the law-tier convention established in Leviticus/Deuteronomy and continued in Matthew. The risen Jesus's closing charge to the disciples (24:44-49) is kept inside Jesus's own manager tier rather than given a separate law tier, since it is a personally embodied scene -- the risen Christ physically present, opening the disciples' understanding and speaking directly to them -- rather than a detached body of transmitted teaching content, per the project's own embodiment test for tier-type choice. Anonymous but textually significant figures (the Widow of Nain, the woman with the issue of blood, the centurion of Capernaum, Jairus, the penitent thief, Barabbas, Cleopas, Simon of Cyrene, and the sinful woman of chapter 7) are kept as unnamed submanagers rather than assigned invented names, per the project's no-invented-identity rule -- this includes explicitly declining to assert the traditional name 'Dismas' for the penitent thief, and explicitly declining to identify the sinful woman of chapter 7 with Mary Magdalene or Mary of Bethany, as textual fact. No verse text is altered, paraphrased, or reinterpreted anywhere in this index -- only described.

scribeTiers.scribeName: The Council of Chief Priests and Scribes

characters.name: Jesus Christ

verses.note: Gabriel announces to Mary that she will conceive by the Holy Ghost and bear a son to be called Jesus.
Born in Bethlehem, wrapped in swaddling clothes, laid in a manger.
Circumcised on the eighth day and named Jesus.
Found in the temple among the doctors at age twelve, hearing and asking questions.
Baptized by John; the Holy Ghost descends as a dove; a voice from heaven declares him the beloved Son.
Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, fasts forty days, and is tempted by the devil.
Reads from Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue, declares it fulfilled, and is rejected by his hometown.

Calls Simon Peter, James, and John to follow him after a miraculous catch of fish; Luke's own account names only Simon and his partners James and John here, not Andrew, unlike the parallel accounts in Matthew 4:18-20 and Mark 1:16-20.
Spends a night in prayer, then chooses the twelve apostles.
Raises the only son of the widow of Nain from the dead, unique to Luke's Gospel.
Eats in the house of Simon the Pharisee; a sinful woman washes his feet with her tears, and he tells her that her sins are forgiven for she loved much.
Feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fishes.
Transfigured on the mountain before Peter, James, and John; Moses and Elias appear.
Steadfastly sets his face to go to Jerusalem.
Teaches the disciples the Lord's Prayer at their request.
Triumphal entry into Jerusalem on a colt.
Institutes the Lord's Supper with the twelve.
Agonizes in prayer at Gethsemane; his sweat is as it were great drops of blood.
Led away to be crucified; the soldiers compel Simon of Cyrene to bear the cross after him.
Crucified at Calvary; prays for his executioners' forgiveness; dies commending his spirit to the Father.
Rises; the women find the tomb empty.
Appears unrecognized to two disciples on the road to Emmaus, and is known to them in the breaking of bread.
Tells the assembled disciples that all things must be fulfilled which were written of him in the law, the prophets, and the psalms, and opens their understanding to understand the scriptures.

Declares that Christ ought to suffer and rise the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem; charges the disciples as witnesses, sends the promise of the Father upon them, and tells them to tarry in Jerusalem until endued with power from on high.
Ascends into heaven from near Bethany.

ageEvents.note: Jesus began to be about thirty years of age when he started his ministry.

funFacts: Luke alone records the age of about thirty at the start of Jesus's ministry (3:23) and the episode of the twelve-year-old Jesus in the Temple (2:41-52), the only childhood incident recorded in any Gospel.

Luke's genealogy of Jesus (3:23-38) runs backward from Jesus to Adam and differs in several names between David and Joseph from Matthew's genealogy -- a real textual divergence between the two Gospels, noted but not resolved here.
Luke's closing charge to the disciples (24:44-49) sets up a thread Luke himself picks up and continues at the start of Acts, his own sequel volume.

characters.name: Zacharias

verses.note: A priest of the course of Abia, married to Elisabeth; both righteous before God, but childless and stricken in years.
While burning incense in the temple, Gabriel appears announcing John's birth; Zacharias doubts and is struck dumb.
At John's circumcision he writes 'His name is John'; his speech is immediately restored.
Filled with the Holy Ghost, prophesies the canticle known as the Benedictus.

funFacts: Belonged to the priestly course of Abia (Abijah), one of the twenty-four priestly divisions established in 1 Chronicles 24:10.
His enforced silence lasted from Gabriel's rebuke until John's naming, roughly the length of Elisabeth's pregnancy.

characters.name: Elisabeth

verses.note: Of the daughters of Aaron; barren and stricken in years.
Conceives and hides herself for five months.
Gabriel tells Mary that her cousin Elisabeth has also conceived in her old age.
Mary visits her; the babe leaps in her womb; filled with the Holy Ghost, she blesses Mary.
Gives birth to John and insists on the name John, against the family's expectation.

funFacts: Called Mary's 'cousin' in the KJV text (Luke 1:36); the exact degree of kinship is not further specified by the text.

characters.name: Gabriel

verses.note: Appears to Zacharias in the temple, announces John's birth, and strikes him mute for unbelief.
Appears to Mary in Nazareth and announces she will conceive Jesus by the Holy Ghost.

funFacts: Names himself only once in the New Testament, to Zacharias: 'I am Gabriel, that stand in the presence of God' (Luke 1:19).
The only angel named in Luke; the angel who appears to the shepherds (2:9-14) is unnamed.

characters.name: Mary the Mother of Jesus

verses.note: Gabriel's annunciation; she answers, 'Be it unto me according to thy word.'
Visits her cousin Elisabeth.
Sings the canticle known as the Magnificat.
Travels to Bethlehem with Joseph and gives birth to Jesus.
Keeps all these sayings, and pondered them in her heart.
Presents Jesus in the temple; Simeon prophesies that a sword shall pierce through her own soul also.
Searches for the twelve-year-old Jesus in Jerusalem for three days.
Comes with Jesus's brothers seeking him; he answers that those who hear and do the word of God are his mother and brethren.

funFacts: Three different women named Mary appear in this book -- Mary the mother of Jesus, Mary Magdalene, and Mary of Bethany -- kept as fully separate entries throughout this index.
The Magnificat (1:46-55) is one of several canticles unique to Luke's birth narrative, alongside Zacharias's Benedictus (1:67-79) and Simeon's Nunc Dimittis (2:29-32).

characters.name: John the Baptist

verses.note: Gabriel foretells his birth and mission, 'in the spirit and power of Elias.'
Born; circumcised and named on the eighth day.
Grows and waxes strong in spirit, in the deserts until his public appearance to Israel.
Begins his wilderness ministry, preaching a baptism of repentance.
Preaches to the multitudes, publicans, and soldiers who come to him.
Denies he is the Christ; foretells one mightier who will baptize with the Holy Ghost and with fire.
Reproves Herod the tetrarch and is shut up in prison.
Sends two disciples from prison to ask Jesus, 'Art thou he that should come?'
Jesus praises him to the multitudes as more than a prophet.
Herod hears of Jesus and is perplexed, having already beheaded John -- his death is referenced, not narrated directly, in Luke.

funFacts: Luke uniquely records John's own birth narrative in parallel with Jesus's, including Zacharias's muteness and the naming controversy (1:57-66).
characters.perkNote: Distinct from John the son of Zebedee, the apostle (a submanager under Simon Peter's tier in this book) -- flagged to avoid confusing the two Johns.

characters.name: The Shepherds of Bethlehem

verses.note: Keeping watch over their flock by night when the angel of the Lord appears to them.
The angel announces the Saviour's birth; a multitude of the heavenly host praises God.
Go with haste to Bethlehem and find Mary, Joseph, and the babe.
Make known abroad the saying told them concerning the child.
Return, glorifying and praising God for all they had heard and seen.

funFacts: Shepherds, not the Magi of Matthew's Gospel, are the first outside witnesses to Jesus's birth in Luke -- the two nativity accounts are kept distinct here.

characters.name: Simeon

verses.note: A just and devout man awaiting the consolation of Israel; the Holy Ghost had revealed he would not see death before seeing the Lord's Christ.
Takes the infant Jesus in his arms and sings the canticle known as the Nunc Dimittis.
Blesses Mary and Joseph; prophesies to Mary that a sword shall pierce through her own soul also.

funFacts: His canticle (2:29-32), beginning 'Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace,' is traditionally called the Nunc Dimittis.

characters.name: Simon Peter

spouses: unnamed wife -- Luke 4:38 (mother-in-law healed), not individually indexed

verses.note: Jesus heals his wife's mother of a great fever.
Miraculous catch of fish; says 'Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord'; leaves all to follow Jesus.
Named first among the twelve apostles, surnamed Peter.
When Jesus asks who touched him amid the crowd, Peter answers on behalf of the group.
Confesses Jesus as 'The Christ of God.'
Present at the Transfiguration; suggests building three tabernacles.
Jesus warns that Satan desires to sift him, and foretells his threefold denial.
Denies Jesus three times; weeps bitterly after the cock crows.
Runs to the empty tomb, stoops down, sees the linen clothes, and wonders.
The risen Lord appears to Simon.

characters.perkNote: Luke's list of the twelve (6:14-16) names 'Judas the brother of James' among the apostles rather than Thaddaeus (as in Matthew/Mark) -- a real naming variation across the Synoptic apostle lists, noted but not resolved here. Distinct from Simon of Cyrene and Simon the Pharisee, also named in this book.

characters.name: Andrew

verses.note: Named among the twelve apostles as 'Andrew his brother' (Simon's brother).

funFacts: Brother of Simon Peter, though Luke's own text does not narrate his individual calling the way it does Peter's -- unlike Matthew 4:18-20 and Mark 1:16-20, Luke's account of the miraculous catch of fish (5:1-11) does not name Andrew as present.

characters.name: James the Son of Zebedee

verses.note: Partner with Peter in the fishing business, called by Jesus.
Named among the twelve, son of Zebedee.
Present at the Transfiguration with Peter and John.
With his brother John, asks Jesus if they should call fire down on a Samaritan village that rejected them.

characters.perkNote: Distinct from James the son of Alphaeus (grouped in the undifferentiated 'Other Apostles' entry below) and from James, the Lord's brother, who is not individually named in Luke.

characters.name: John the Son of Zebedee

verses.note: Partner with Peter and his brother James in the fishing business, called by Jesus.
Named among the twelve.
Present at the Transfiguration.
Reports forbidding a man who cast out devils in Jesus's name because he did not follow with them; Jesus corrects him.
With James, asks to call fire down on a Samaritan village.
Sent with Peter to prepare the Passover.

characters.perkNote: Distinct from John the Baptist, who has his own full manager tier in this book -- flagged to avoid confusing the two Johns.

characters.name: Levi (Matthew)

verses.note: A publican named Levi, sitting at the receipt of custom, is called by Jesus and leaves all to follow him.
Makes Jesus a great feast in his own house.

funFacts: Called 'Levi' in Luke's own account of his calling (5:27); identified with the apostle Matthew of Luke 6:15 by comparison with the parallel accounts in Matthew's own Gospel.

characters.name: The Other Apostles

verses.note: Named in the full list of the twelve: Philip, Bartholomew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Simon called Zelotes, and Judas the brother of James.

funFacts: Luke's text gives no individually differentiated action to these six apostles beyond their inclusion in the list of the twelve (6:14-16); kept as one collective entry rather than inventing individual roles the text doesn't support.
characters.perkNote: Includes 'Simon called Zelotes' (6:15) -- distinct from Simon Peter, Simon of Cyrene, and Simon the Pharisee; at least four men named Simon appear across this book, flagged here per the project's naming-collision rule.

characters.name: Judas Iscariot

verses.note: Named last among the twelve, 'which also was the traitor.'
Satan enters into Judas; he covenants with the chief priests and captains to betray Jesus for money.
Jesus announces at the Supper that his betrayer's hand is with him on the table.
Betrays Jesus with a kiss in Gethsemane: 'Judas, betrayest thou the Son of man with a kiss?'

funFacts: Unlike Matthew, Luke does not state the sum of money paid to Judas, only that 'they covenanted to give him money' (22:5).

characters.name: Zacchaeus

verses.note: Chief among the publicans, rich, and of short stature, climbs a sycomore tree to see Jesus passing through Jericho.
Jesus calls him down and invites himself to his house; Zacchaeus receives him joyfully.
The crowd murmurs that Jesus has gone to be guest with a sinner.
Pledges half his goods to the poor and to restore fourfold anything taken by false accusation.
Jesus declares salvation has come to his house: 'the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.'

funFacts: Zacchaeus's story is unique to Luke's Gospel, fitting the book's recurring emphasis on outcasts and the marginalized.

characters.name: Martha of Bethany

verses.note: Receives Jesus into her house.
Cumbered about much serving; complains that her sister has left her to serve alone.
Jesus answers, 'Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things... Mary hath chosen that good part.'

funFacts: This Martha and Mary of Bethany are distinct from Mary the mother of Jesus and from Mary Magdalene -- three different Marys appear across this book, kept as separate entries throughout.
Their brother Lazarus is not mentioned in this passage in Luke -- the raising of Lazarus is recorded only in John's Gospel, not here.

characters.name: Mary of Bethany

verses.note: Sits at Jesus's feet and hears his word.
Jesus says she has chosen the good part, which shall not be taken from her.

funFacts: Sister of Martha of Bethany; a third, distinct Mary in this book alongside Mary the mother of Jesus and Mary Magdalene.

characters.name: Mary Magdalene

verses.note: Healed of evil spirits and infirmities; seven devils had gone out of her.
Among the women who ministered unto Jesus of their substance.
With the women who followed from Galilee, beholds the crucifixion and where Jesus's body is laid.
Comes to the tomb with spices, finds it empty, sees the two men in shining garments, and reports to the apostles.

characters.perkNote: Not identified in Luke's text with the sinful woman of chapter 7 or with Mary of Bethany -- a traditional but text-unsupported conflation, not asserted here as fact.

spouses: unnamed reference: wife of Chuza, Herod's steward -- Luke 8:3, not individually indexed

verses.note: Wife of Chuza, Herod's steward; ministers to Jesus of her substance.
Among the women who report the empty tomb to the apostles.
Named among the women who ministered to Jesus of their substance.

characters.name: Mary the Mother of James

verses.note: Named among the women at the empty tomb who report to the apostles.

characters.perkNote: Distinct from Mary the mother of Jesus, Mary Magdalene, and Mary of Bethany -- the fourth distinct Mary named in this book.

characters.name: Herod Antipas

genealogy.father: Herod the Great -- not individually indexed in this book

verses.note: Tetrarch of Galilee.
Reproved by John the Baptist for Herodias and other evils; shuts John up in prison.
Hears of Jesus's works and is perplexed, having beheaded John; desires to see Jesus.
Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod seeks to kill him; Jesus calls him 'that fox.'

Pilate sends Jesus to Herod as a Galilean during the trial; Herod questions him, Jesus answers nothing, Herod and his men of war mock him and send him back arrayed in a gorgeous robe; Herod and Pilate become friends that day.

characters.perkNote: Same individual as the Herod Antipas who executes John the Baptist in Matthew's Gospel (there only a submanager under John the Baptist's tier); promoted to a full manager tier in this book given his expanded, unique role across Luke's narrative, including the trial scene before him found only in Luke (23:6-12). Distinct from Herod the Great (Matthew's nativity-era king) and from Herod Agrippa (of Acts).

verses.note: Governor of Judaea.
Reported to have mingled the blood of certain Galilaeans with their sacrifices.
The multitude brings Jesus to Pilate; Pilate finds no fault in him.
Learns Jesus is of Herod's jurisdiction and sends him to Herod.
Declares to the chief priests and rulers that neither he nor Herod found Jesus guilty of anything worthy of death; proposes to chastise and release him.
Yields to the crowd's demand, releases Barabbas, and delivers Jesus to their will.
The multitude cries out to release Barabbas, who for a certain sedition and murder had been cast into prison.
Pilate releases him unto them.

characters.name: The Council of Chief Priests and Scribes
characters.scribeTier: The Council of Chief Priests and Scribes

verses.note: Annas and Caiaphas named as the high priests at the start of John's ministry.
Chief priests, scribes, and the chief of the people seek to destroy Jesus but fear the people.
Chief priests and scribes challenge Jesus's authority and send spies to entangle him in his talk.
Chief priests and scribes seek how they might kill Jesus, fearing the people.
Chief priests, captains of the temple, and elders come to arrest Jesus in Gethsemane; he is led to the high priest's house.
The elders, chief priests, and scribes assemble, question Jesus, and lead him to Pilate.
Chief priests and scribes vehemently accuse Jesus before Herod.

funFacts: Annas and Caiaphas are named together as the ruling high priests in 3:2, but neither is individually characterized in action within Luke's own text the way Caiaphas is in Matthew's trial account -- treated here as part of the collective council rather than given a separate personal tier.

characters.name: The Ten Lepers

verses.note: Ten leprous men meet Jesus, stand afar off, and cry, 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us.'
Jesus tells them to show themselves to the priests; as they went, they were cleansed.
One of them, seeing he was healed, turns back glorifying God and falls at Jesus's feet giving thanks -- he was a Samaritan.
Jesus asks where the other nine are, and tells the man, 'thy faith hath made thee whole.'

funFacts: The text differentiates only one of the ten by description -- 'a Samaritan' -- not by name; the other nine are never distinguished individually, so all ten are kept as one collective entry rather than inventing separate identities.

characters.name: Joseph

children: jesus_luke -- legal/adoptive father, not by blood per Luke 1:34-35

verses.note: Espoused to Mary, of the house of David.
Goes up from Galilee to Bethlehem, being of the house and lineage of David, with Mary his espoused wife.
Found by the shepherds with Mary and the babe.
Brings Jesus to the temple to perform the custom of the law.
Goes to Jerusalem for the Passover; with Mary, seeks the twelve-year-old Jesus for three days.

funFacts: Jesus's genealogy in Luke (3:23-38) is traced through Joseph, described as 'as was supposed' the son of Joseph, back to Heli and ultimately to Adam -- the text itself flags this as a matter of legal/supposed descent, consistent with the virgin birth stated in 1:34-35.

characters.name: The Penitent Thief

verses.note: One of the two malefactors crucified with Jesus rebukes the other for railing on him, says 'we receive the due reward of our deeds,' and asks Jesus to remember him in his kingdom; Jesus answers, 'To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.'

characters.perkNote: Unnamed in the biblical text; later Christian tradition gives him the name 'Dismas,' which is not asserted here as textual fact.

characters.name: Cleopas

verses.note: Two disciples walk to Emmaus discussing the crucifixion, one named Cleopas; the risen Jesus joins them unrecognized and expounds the scriptures.
Jesus is made known to them in the breaking of bread, then vanishes out of their sight.
They return to Jerusalem and tell the eleven.

characters.perkNote: Cleopas's companion on the road is not named in the text; not assigned an identity here.

children: unnamed daughter -- Luke 8:42, about twelve years of age, not individually indexed

verses.note: A ruler of the synagogue falls at Jesus's feet, beseeching him to come to his house for his only daughter, about twelve years old, lying at the point of death.
Told his daughter is dead; Jesus tells him, 'Fear not: believe only, and she shall be made whole.'
Jesus raises the child, saying, 'Maid, arise.'

characters.name: The Woman with the Issue of Blood

verses.note: A woman with an issue of blood for twelve years, unable to be healed by any physician, touches the border of Jesus's garment and is immediately healed.
Jesus perceives that virtue has gone out of him; she confesses before all the people; he tells her, 'Daughter, be of good comfort: thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace.'
His servant, who is dear to him, is sick and ready to die; elders of the Jews beseech Jesus on his behalf, saying he loves the nation and built them a synagogue.
Sends friends saying he is not worthy that Jesus should enter his roof, but to speak the word only, as a man himself under authority.
Jesus marvels and says, 'I have not found so great faith, no, not in Israel'; the servant is healed.

characters.name: The Widow of Nain

children: unnamed son -- Luke 7:12, not individually indexed

verses.note: Jesus meets a funeral procession at Nain for her only son; she is a widow, and Jesus has compassion, saying 'Weep not.'
Jesus touches the bier and says, 'Young man, I say unto thee, Arise'; the dead man sits up and speaks, and Jesus delivers him to his mother.
The people glorify God, saying, 'A great prophet is risen up among us.'

funFacts: Unnamed in the text; the raising of her son is unique to Luke's Gospel among the four.

characters.name: Simon of Cyrene

verses.note: As Jesus is led away to be crucified, the soldiers lay hold on Simon, a Cyrenian, coming out of the country, and compel him to bear the cross after Jesus.

funFacts: Luke does not state why Simon was compelled to carry the cross beyond that he was 'coming out of the country' and was seized by those leading Jesus away; the text gives no further detail about him.
characters.perkNote: Distinct from Simon Peter, Simon the Pharisee, and Simon called Zelotes -- at least four men named Simon appear across this book, flagged per the project's naming-collision rule.

characters.name: Simon the Pharisee

verses.note: A Pharisee named Simon desires Jesus to eat with him; Jesus goes into his house and sits down to meat.
Seeing a sinful woman anoint Jesus's feet, he says within himself that if Jesus were a prophet he would know what manner of woman this is.
Jesus answers him with the parable of the two debtors, asking which debtor loved the creditor more; Simon answers, 'he to whom he forgave most.'
Jesus contrasts Simon's lack of hospitality (no water for his feet, no kiss, no oil) with the woman's tears, kisses, and ointment.
Jesus declares her many sins are forgiven, 'for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little.'

characters.perkNote: Distinct from Simon Peter, Simon of Cyrene, and Simon called Zelotes -- at least four men named Simon appear across this book, flagged per the project's naming-collision rule.

characters.name: The Sinful Woman

verses.note: A woman in the city, described as a sinner, brings an alabaster box of ointment, stands at Jesus's feet weeping, washes them with her tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them with the ointment.
Jesus points to her tears, kisses, and ointment as a contrast to Simon the Pharisee's lack of hospitality.
Jesus tells her that her sins, which are many, are forgiven, 'for she loved much.'
Jesus tells her, 'Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.'

characters.perkNote: Unnamed in the text; not identified here with Mary Magdalene or Mary of Bethany -- a traditional but text-unsupported identification, not asserted as fact.

characters.name: Anna the Prophetess

spouses: unnamed husband -- Luke 2:36, married seven years, deceased; not individually indexed

verses.note: A prophetess, daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser, of great age, having lived with a husband seven years from her virginity.
A widow of about fourscore and four years; departs not from the temple, but serves God with fastings and prayers night and day.
Comes in at the moment of Jesus's presentation, gives thanks, and speaks of him to all that looked for redemption in Jerusalem.

funFacts: One of only two named prophetic voices to recognize the infant Jesus in the temple, alongside Simeon.
characters.perkNote: Attached to Jesus's own tier rather than Simeon's: Luke 2:25-38 depicts Anna and Simeon as two independent witnesses in the same temple scene with no textual relationship, interaction, or kinship stated between them. Anna's real textual connection is to the infant Jesus, of whom she speaks to onlookers, not to Simeon.

characters.name: The Sermon on the Plain
characters.purpose: Jesus's core ethical teaching to his disciples and a great multitude, delivered standing 'in the plain' (6:17) rather than on a mountain as in Matthew's parallel -- the Beatitudes paired with corresponding Woes, teaching on loving enemies and not judging others, and the closing parable of the two builders, framing what it means to truly hear and do his words.

verses.note: Jesus stands in the plain with his disciples and a great multitude.
The Beatitudes: blessed are the poor, the hungry, those that weep, and the hated and reproached.
The corresponding Woes: woe unto the rich, the full, those that laugh, and those spoken well of.
Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you, and the Golden Rule.
Judge not; the parable of the mote and the beam.
A good tree is known by its fruit.
The parable of the wise and foolish builders.

funFacts: Luke's Beatitudes (6:20-23) are paired with four corresponding Woes (6:24-26) not found in Matthew's Sermon on the Mount.

characters.name: The Commissioning of the Seventy
characters.purpose: Jesus appoints and sends out a wider group of disciples beyond the twelve, two by two, into every city he intended to visit -- instructing them on dependence, urgency, and the authority given them, and rejoicing when they return with reports of power over devils.

verses.note: Appoints seventy others and sends them two and two before his face.
Instructions: the harvest is plenteous, go as lambs among wolves, carry no purse, scrip, or shoes, eat such things as are set before you, and a warning for towns that reject them.
Woes pronounced on Chorazin, Bethsaida, and Capernaum for their unbelief.
The seventy return with joy, reporting even the devils are subject to them; Jesus tells them to rejoice rather that their names are written in heaven.
Jesus rejoices in spirit, thanking the Father for revealing these things to babes.

funFacts: This wider sending of seventy (some manuscripts read seventy-two) disciples is unique to Luke's Gospel among the four.

characters.name: The Good Samaritan
characters.purpose: Told in answer to a lawyer's question, 'And who is my neighbour?' -- redefines neighborly love across ethnic and religious lines by making a despised Samaritan, not the priest or Levite, the example of mercy.

verses.note: A certain lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, then asks, 'who is my neighbour?'
The parable: a man falls among thieves; a priest and a Levite pass by; a Samaritan has compassion, binds his wounds, and pays for his care at an inn.
Jesus asks which was neighbour; the lawyer answers, 'he that shewed mercy'; Jesus says, 'Go, and do thou likewise.'

characters.name: Parables of the Lost
characters.purpose: Told to Pharisees and scribes who murmured that Jesus received sinners and ate with them -- three linked parables (a lost sheep, a lost coin, and a lost son) each ending in joy and celebration, teaching that heaven rejoices over one sinner that repents.

verses.note: Publicans and sinners draw near to hear Jesus; Pharisees and scribes murmur.
The lost sheep: a shepherd leaves the ninety and nine to seek the one that is lost, and rejoices when he finds it.
The lost coin: a woman sweeps her house to find one lost piece of silver, and rejoices with her neighbours.

The prodigal son: a younger son wastes his inheritance in riotous living, returns in repentance, and is received by his father with a robe, a ring, and a feast; the elder son's resentment is answered by the father.

funFacts: The parable of the prodigal son (15:11-32) is unique to Luke and among the most extensively developed parables in any Gospel.

characters.name: Lazarus and the Rich Man
characters.purpose: A parable warning of a fixed reversal of fortune after death for the wealthy who neglect the poor at their gate, and affirming that even a resurrection from the dead would not persuade those unwilling to hear Moses and the prophets.

verses.note: A certain rich man clothed in purple and fine linen; a beggar named Lazarus, full of sores, laid at his gate, desiring the crumbs from his table.
Both die; the beggar is carried by angels into Abraham's bosom; the rich man is in torment in hell.
The rich man begs Abraham for relief; told a great gulf is fixed between them.
The rich man asks that Lazarus warn his five brethren; Abraham answers they have Moses and the prophets, and would not be persuaded though one rose from the dead.

funFacts: This parable's beggar is named 'Lazarus' -- a distinct figure from Lazarus of Bethany, whose raising is recorded only in John's Gospel (not in Luke at all); the two are not the same person and are not connected in the text.

characters.name: Parables of Prayer and Humility
characters.purpose: Two parables told together on how one ought to pray and regard oneself before God -- persistence in prayer illustrated by an unjust judge worn down by a widow's request, and true humility illustrated by a Pharisee's boasting prayer contrasted with a publican's plea for mercy.

verses.note: The unjust judge, who feared not God nor regarded man, is wearied by a widow's continual pleading and avenges her.
Jesus's application: shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him?
Told unto certain which trusted in themselves that they were righteous: a Pharisee stands and prays, thanking God he is not as other men.

A publican, standing afar off, will not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smites his breast, saying 'God be merciful to me a sinner'; Jesus says this man went down to his house justified rather than the other.

characters.name: The Parable of the Pounds
characters.purpose: Told because Jesus was near Jerusalem and the people supposed the kingdom of God should immediately appear -- a nobleman entrusts ten servants with a pound each before departing to receive a kingdom, teaching faithful stewardship and accountability while awaiting the master's return.

verses.note: A certain nobleman goes into a far country to receive a kingdom, delivers ten pounds to ten servants, saying 'Occupy till I come.'
His citizens hate him and refuse his reign; on his return he rewards the servants who gained ten and five pounds with cities to rule.
A servant who hid his pound in a napkin out of fear is rebuked.
His pound is given to the one who has ten; the nobleman's enemies who would not have him reign are slain before him.

funFacts: Distinct from Matthew's Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), which uses larger, unequal sums and a different structure -- the two parables are related in theme but not identical, and are kept as separate content here.

genealogyLists.note: Bulk or deliberately-unresolved references, kept out of the character list above.

genealogyOfJesusLuke.note: Jesus's genealogy as traced ('as was supposed') through Joseph back through Heli to Adam and to God -- runs in the opposite direction from Matthew's genealogy (which runs forward from Abraham to Joseph) and differs in several names between David and Joseph. Not individually indexed here; the underlying Old Testament figures shared with Matthew's genealogy are already covered in the Genesis/Ruth/Samuel/Kings/Chronicles character indexes.

seventyDisciples.note: The seventy (or seventy-two, per manuscript variation) disciples sent out in pairs are never individually named in the text; represented collectively by the Commissioning of the Seventy law tier rather than as separate characters.

womenWhoMinistered.note: 'Many others' beyond Mary Magdalene, Joanna, and Susanna are said to have ministered to Jesus of their substance, but are not named and are not individually indexed.
